title: Two q-analogues of permutations
key_idea: There are two natural $q$-analogues of the symmetric group $\mathfrak{S}_n$: (1) invertible linear transformations $\text{GL}(n,q)$ on $\mathbb{F}_q^n$ (permutations as bijections), and (2) maximal chains (flags) in $\mathbb{F}_q^n$ ($q$-analogues of permutations as words/chains). The cycle indicator of $\text{Mat}(n,q)$ and the formula for $c_f(\lambda)$ are the $q$-analogues of Theorem 1.3.3 and Proposition 1.3.2.
summary: Section 1.10 develops two $q$-analogues of $\mathfrak{S}_n$. In §1.10.1, $\text{GL}(n,q)$ plays the role of $\mathfrak{S}_n$: the order of $\text{GL}(n,q)$ is a $q$-analogue of $n!$ (Prop 1.10.1). The adjoint action on $\text{Mat}(n,q)$ gives an orbit structure counted by $\omega(n,q) = \sum_j p_j(n)q^j$ (Prop 1.10.2). Theorem 1.10.4 is the $q$-analogue of the cycle indicator generating function. In §1.10.2, flags in $\mathbb{F}_q^n$ are the $q$-analogue of words/permutations, giving the $q$-analogue of descent statistics.

notation.description: General linear group: invertible $n\times n$ matrices over $\mathbb{F}_q$
Cycle indicator of $\text{Mat}(n,q)$ — $q$-analogue of the cycle indicator $Z_n(t_i)$
# matrices in $\text{GL}$ commuting with a fixed matrix of orbit type $\lambda$ for irreducible $f$

definitions.statement:
The **general linear group** $\text{GL}(n,q)$ is the group of all invertible $n\times n$ matrices over $\mathbb{F}_q$. It is the $q$-analogue of the symmetric group $\mathfrak{S}_n$ (permutations as bijections).

The **orbit type** $\Phi_M: \mathcal{I}(K) \to \text{Par}$ of a matrix $M \in \text{Mat}(n,K)$ assigns to each monic irreducible polynomial $f$ the partition $\lambda(f)$ such that the $f$-primary component of $K[M]$ as a $K[u]$-module has type $\lambda(f)$. This is the $q$-analogue of the cycle type.

propositions.title: Order of GL(n,q)
propositions.proof_sketch: An invertible $n\times n$ matrix has rows that are linearly independent. The first row can be any nonzero vector ($q^n-1$ choices), the second can be any vector not in the span of the first ($q^n - q$ choices), etc.

propositions.title: Conjugacy classes and partitions
propositions.statement: The number of orbits $\omega(n,q)$ of $\text{GL}(n,q)$ acting adjointly on $\text{Mat}(n,q)$ (equivalently, the number of conjugacy classes of $\text{Mat}(n,q)$) satisfies $$\omega(n,q) = \sum_j p_j(n)q^j,$$ where $p_j(n)$ is the number of partitions of $n$ into exactly $j$ parts. Equivalently, $\sum_{n\geq 0}\omega(n,q)x^n = \prod_{j\geq 1}(1-qx^j)^{-1}.$
propositions.proof_sketch: Apply Theorem 1.10.4 with the cycle indicator. The number of irreducible polynomials of degree $d$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$ is $\beta(d,q) = \frac{1}{d}\sum_{e|d}\mu(d/e)q^e$. Computing the resulting product expansion yields the partition GF.

theorems.title: q-analogue of cycle indicator GF
theorems.statement: Let $Z_n(t;q)$ be the cycle indicator of $\text{Mat}(n,q)$ (defined by analogy with $Z_n(t_i)$). Then $$\sum_{n\geq 0} Z_n(t;q)x^n = \prod_{f\in\mathcal{I}}\sum_{\lambda\in\text{Par}} \frac{t_{f,\lambda}\,x^{|\lambda|\cdot\text{deg}(f)}}{c_f(\lambda)},$$ where $c_f(\lambda)$ is the number of matrices in $\text{GL}$ commuting with a fixed matrix of orbit type $\{f\mapsto\lambda\}$.
theorems.proof_sketch: By Burnside's lemma (equation 1.106), the number of orbits of $\text{GL}(n,q)$ on $\text{Mat}(n,q)$ factors. The orbit type decomposes into a product over irreducible polynomials $f$, each factor independent. The formula follows by combining the GF for each factor.

theorems.title: Formula for $c_f(\lambda)$
theorems.statement: Let $f \in \mathcal{I}(K)$ have degree $d$, and let $\lambda \vdash n$ with conjugate $\lambda'$ and $m_i = m_i(\lambda) = \lambda'_i - \lambda'_{i+1}$. Set $h_i = \lambda'_1+\cdots+\lambda'_i$. Then $$c_f(\lambda) = \prod_{i\geq 1}\prod_{j=1}^{m_i}(q^{h_i d} - q^{(h_i-j)d}).$$
theorems.proof_sketch: Count the indexed bases for $\mathbb{F}_q^{nd}$ that define a matrix $M$ with $\Phi_M(f)=\lambda$. The counting of valid choices for each basis vector $v_{ij}$ in the flag decomposition gives the product formula.

corollaries.title: Diagonalizable matrices GF
corollaries.statement: Let $d_n$ = number of diagonalizable (over $\mathbb{F}_q$) matrices $M \in \text{Mat}(n,q)$. Then $$\sum_{n\geq 0} d_n \frac{x^n}{\gamma(n)} = \left(\sum_{k\geq 0}\frac{x^k}{\gamma(k)}\right)^q.$$
corollaries.proof_sketch: Specialize Theorem 1.10.4 using that $M$ is diagonalizable iff $\Phi_M(f) = \langle 1^k\rangle$ for each linear $f=z-a$ (with $k$ = multiplicity of eigenvalue $a$) and $\Phi_M(f)=\emptyset$ for non-linear $f$.

corollaries.title: Nilpotent matrices
corollaries.statement:
(a) $\frac{1}{1-x} = \prod_{n\geq 1}\prod_{r\geq 1}(1-q^{rn}x^n)^{-\beta^*(n,q)}$.
(b) The number of nilpotent matrices $M \in \text{Mat}(n,q)$ is $g(n) = q^{n(n-1)}$.
corollaries.proof_sketch: (b) follows by specializing Corollary 1.10.10 to $t_z=0$ (no copies of $f=z$) and $t_f=1$ for $f\neq z$, reducing to a partition identity from Proposition 1.8.6(a).

exercises.statement: Prove directly that the number of nilpotent matrices in $\text{Mat}(n,q)$ is $q^{n(n-1)}$.
hints: A matrix is nilpotent iff it has all eigenvalues equal to 0 iff its characteristic polynomial is $z^n$. Use the orbit-type formula.

text_passages.text: The $n$-element set $[n]$ is replaced by $\mathbb{F}_q^n$ (an $n$-dimensional vector space). A bijection $[n]\to[n]$ corresponds to an invertible linear map $\mathbb{F}_q^n \to \mathbb{F}_q^n$. The 'group of bijections' $\mathfrak{S}_n$ corresponds to $\text{GL}(n,q)$.

The **orbit type** of $M \in \text{Mat}(n,K)$ generalizes cycle type: it assigns to each monic irreducible polynomial $f$ a partition $\lambda(f)$ (from the $K[u]$-module structure). This is the $q$-analogue of the cycle type of a permutation.

text_passages.label: Proposition 1.10.2 — Conjugacy classes
text_passages.preview: The number of $\text{GL}(n,q)$ orbits on $\text{Mat}(n,q)$ is $\omega(n,q) = \sum_j p_j(n)q^j$, a satisfactory $q$-analogue of $p(n)$ (the number of conjugacy classes of $\mathfrak{S}_n$).

text_passages.label: Theorem 1.10.7 — Formula for $c_f(\lambda)$
text_passages.preview: $c_f(\lambda) = \prod_{i\geq 1}\prod_{j=1}^{m_i}(q^{h_id}-q^{(h_i-j)d})$. This is the $q$-analogue of Proposition 1.3.2 (cycle type count formula).

text_passages.label: Corollary 1.10.11 — Nilpotent matrices
text_passages.preview: The number of nilpotent $n\times n$ matrices over $\mathbb{F}_q$ is $g(n)=q^{n(n-1)}$. Follows from the cycle indicator specialization and Prop 1.8.6(a).
